November 2019

modalities.value: text (language model generating paragraphs of text)

source.quote:
GPT-2 is a large-scale unsupervised language model that generates coherent paragraphs of text, first
announced by OpenAI in February 2019 [65].

languages.value: Primarily English; training data filtered to documents at least 50% English; French about 0.025% of dataset

source.quote:
GPT-2’s training data was filtered to remove documents where content was less than 50% English-
language. However, it can output other languages with varying levels of coherence. GPT-2 can perform
basic translations in French, with French accounting for 0.025% of the dataset [65].

totalParams.value: Four variants: 124 million, 355 million, 774 million, and ~1.5 billion parameters

source.quote:
We developed four variants of the model, ranging in
size from small (124 million parameters) to large (~1.5 billion parameters).

GPT-2 is a large-scale unsupervised language model that generates coherent paragraphs of text, first
announced by OpenAI in February 2019 [65].

trainingData.value: WebText (internet-scale English web text; top domains include Google, Archive.org, Blogspot, GitHub, NYT, etc.)

source.quote:
We have published a list of the top 1,000 sources
in the ‘WebText’ dataset that GPT-2 was trained on to facilitate further study by researchers here [57].

riskDecisions.labLabel: minimal evidence of misuse so far; confidence in publishing 774M and 1.5B

source.quote:
In addi-
tion to finding minimal evidence of misuse so far, several other factors contributed to our confidence
in publishing our 774 million and 1.5 billion parameter models.

topics.headline: Threat monitoring found discussion of misuse but no clear large-scale misuse or malicious code sharing; spam/phishing of interest to lower-tier actors

source.quote:
We also found no clear malicious code sharing or large-scale misuse, and only a small number of
cases of explicit public plans for misuse.

topics.headline: Exploratory bias probes for gender, race, religion, and language preference; no significant size differences except language preference for 1.5B

source.quote:
We did not see
statistically significant differences in our gender, race, or religion bias analyses between our 774 million
and 1.5 billion parameter models. Language preference bias changed with the 1.5 billion parameter
model

topics.headline: Human credibility of cherry-picked GPT-2 fake news ~66% (355M) and ~75% (774M/1.5B); automated detection of synthetic text studied

source.quote:
Kreps and McCain at Cornell University found that cherry-picked fake
news samples from the 355 million parameter version of GPT-2 were considered “credible” about 66%
of the time.

topics.headline: Public discussion of GPT-2 for spam and phishing; no observed progress beyond discussion for lower-tier actors

source.quote:
We have seen some discussion around GPT-2’s potential to augment high-volume/low-yield operations
like spam and phishing. However, we have not seen any progress (evidence of writing code or documen-
tation) toward realizing this beyond discussion.

testers.name: Cornell University
testers.scope: Human susceptibility to GPT-2-generated digital disinformation; perceived credibility of synthesized news

source.quote:
Cornell University is studying human susceptibility to digital disinformation generated by
          language models.

testers.name: Middlebury Institute of International Studies Center on Terrorism, Extremism, and Counterterrorism (CTEC)
testers.scope: How GPT-2 could be misused by terrorists and extremists; fine-tuning on extremist datasets and detection

source.quote:
The Middlebury Institute of International Studies Center on Terrorism, Extremism, and
          Counterterrorism (CTEC) is exploring how GPT-2 could be misused by terrorists and extremists
          online.

testers.name: University of Oregon
testers.scope: Bias probes to analyze bias within GPT-2

source.quote: The University of Oregon is developing a series of “bias probes” to analyze bias within GPT-2.

testers.name: University of Texas at Austin
testers.scope: Statistical detectability of GPT-2 outputs after fine-tuning; detection transfer across language models

source.quote:
The University of Texas at Austin is studying the statistical detectability of GPT-2 outputs af-
          ter fine-tuning the model on domain-specific datasets, as well as the extent of detection transfer
          across different language models.

findings.text: Staged release withheld larger GPT-2 models for nine months after the February 2019 announcement due to misuse concerns such as fake news, email impersonation, and abusive social media automation.

source.quote:
We chose a staged release
process, releasing the smallest model in February, but withholding larger models due to concerns about
the potential for misuse, such as generating fake news content, impersonating others in email, or au-
tomating abusive social media content production [56].

findings.text: Zero-shot probability-threshold detection of Top-K 40 generations with the 1.5B model was only between 83% and 85% accuracy, underperforming the N-gram baseline.

source.quote:
the
1.5 billion parameter GPT-2 model can detect Top-K 40 generations with between 83% and 85% ac-
curacy. This underperforms relative to our N-gram based baseline

findings.text: CTEC reported that GPT-2 fine-tuned on extremist material relatively quickly integrates ideological nuances and can produce substantively consistent text.

source.quote:
In their own words, their results suggest that “GPT-2 relatively quickly
integrates the nuances of the ideology it is trained on when responding to a specific prompt,” and that
“fine-tuned GPT-2 models can produce substantively consistent text.”

findings.text: Fine-tuning on narrow datasets increased perceived humanness of GPT-2 text and reduced GROVER zero-shot detection of fine-tuned outputs.

source.quote:
our partners at the Middlebury Institute’s Center on Terrorism, Extremism, and Counterterror-
ism have confirmed that fine-tuning GPT-2 on more narrow datasets tends to increase the perceived
humanness of GPT-2-generated text.

findings.text: In Cornell’s automated-cleaning study, none of the survey respondents who called articles “fake news” said they believed the story lacked a human author.

source.quote:
while a number of respondents wrote that they thought the article may have
  been “fake news,” none indicated that they believed the story did not have a human
  author.

notes: Source is the November 2019 arXiv PDF (1908.09203), 71 PDF pages. Printed page numbers used for the main report; Appendix E (Cornell) and Appendix C restart page numbers—Cornell credibility means cite Appendix E printed page 3. No modern risk framework (ASL/Preparedness); one staged-release decision under manipulation. Chart-only Figures 1–2 and Appendix C bias bar counts skipped (no reliable color/row mapping). Ranges 83–85% put in findings, not evalResults. Intermediate TF-IDF scores for 355M/774M not stated. Partner license in Appendix A is not a public model license. Public GPT-2 license, context window, and training compute not stated in this report.
